envy.label: Envy and comparison
envy.insight: The cure for envy in the Quran and Sunnah begins by changing the direction of one's gaze: “Look at those below you and do not look at those above you, for that is more likely to keep you from belittling Allah's favours upon you,” then turning wishing into striving: “And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others… and ask Allah of His bounty.” Praiseworthy longing is only in matters of goodness. And the highest level: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his brother what he likes for himself.”

now: Say quietly about the person you envy: “O Allah, bless him”
Write down five blessings you have
week: Reduce your exposure to what triggers comparison (certain accounts, certain gatherings)
Turn the envy into a plan: what can I strive for out of what they have?
long: Pray for good for the person you envy until your heart settles
Build your contentment on your relationship with Allah, not on your ranking among people

questions: Do I wish their blessing would disappear, or do I wish for something like it?
What do I not see of their life?
avoid: Backbiting and belittling the person you envy

evil_eye.label: The evil eye and others' envy
evil_eye.insight: The evil eye is real, as the Prophet ﷺ said, and protection from it is through spiritual safeguarding, not fear: the last two surahs of the Quran (“no one has sought refuge with anything like them”), the morning and evening remembrances, and lawful ruqyah. And whoever admires something should pray for blessing: “Why did you not pray for blessing when you saw what you liked?” But the Prophetic way warns against explaining every problem by the evil eye or magic and neglecting natural and medical causes.

now: Recite the last two surahs, al-Fatihah and Ayat al-Kursi, and blow lightly over yourself
Say three times: “In the name of Allah, with whose name nothing can cause harm…”
week: Keep up the morning and evening remembrances
If the symptoms are physical or psychological, see a doctor first
long: Do not attach yourself to healers who ask for things contrary to the Shariah
Trust in Allah is the strongest protection

questions: Have I looked into the medical and natural causes?
Has fear of the evil eye started to disrupt my life?
avoid: Accusing people of envy without evidence

comparison.label: Comparison and social media
comparison.insight: “And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to some categories of them, the splendour of worldly life” — a flower is beautiful but quick to wither. The Quran describes this world as “boasting to one another and competition in increase.” The Sunnah turns the scale of comparison around: in worldly matters look at those below you, and in religion at those above you. And “Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth, but He looks to your hearts and your deeds.”

now: Close the app that is triggering comparison, now
Write down three blessings that are yours
week: Set a limited daily time for social media
Unfollow the accounts that make you feel inadequate
long: Set your goals by your own standards, not other people's
Remember: people only show their best moments

questions: Am I comparing my real inner life with their curated outside?
If I had not seen anyone's life, would I feel inadequate?
avoid: Measuring your worth by likes and followers
Overspending to keep up with others

gratitude.label: Gratitude and blessings
gratitude.insight: In the Quran gratitude brings increase (“if you are grateful, I will surely increase you”), and the Prophet ﷺ stood in prayer until his feet swelled and said: “Should I not be a grateful servant?” In times of ease the believer is grateful, and that is good for him. Success is a test just like failure: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult over what He has given you,” and at the moment of victory, at the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ entered humbly with his head lowered.

now: Make a prostration of thanks to Allah
Say: “O Allah, whatever blessing I have this morning is from You alone, You have no partner”
week: Thank those who were a means of the blessing (“he who does not thank people does not thank Allah”)
Give charity as thanks to Allah
long: Use the blessing in obedience to Allah
Be humble in success

questions: How can I use this blessing in what pleases Allah?
Who helped me whom I have not thanked?
avoid: Attributing the blessing to yourself alone

illness.label: Illness and health
illness.insight: In the Sunnah, illness is expiation and elevation: “No fatigue or illness befalls a Muslim… except that Allah expiates some of his sins by it,” and the sick person is credited with what he used to do when healthy. Seeking treatment is commanded: “Seek treatment, for Allah has not made a disease without appointing a remedy for it.” Complaining to Allah does not contradict patience, as Ayyub prayed: “Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.” And the sick person has a Prophetic ruqyah: place your hand where it hurts and say “Bismillah” three times and “I seek refuge with Allah and His power from the evil of what I feel and what I fear” seven times.

now: Place your hand where it hurts and say: Bismillah (3 times); I seek refuge with Allah and His power from the evil of what I feel and what I fear (7 times)
Follow the doctor's instructions and your medication
week: Get a second medical opinion if you are unsure
Stay in touch with those who support you and do not isolate yourself
Pray as you are able: standing, sitting or lying on your side
long: Seek the reward, and remember that your usual worship is still being recorded for you
Look after your mental health alongside your physical health

questions: Am I dealing with the illness using all the medical means?
What could give meaning to this stage of my life?
avoid: Abandoning treatment in the name of trust in Allah

study.label: Studies and exams
study.insight: The “strong believer” hadith in Muslim sums it all up: “Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say ‘if only I had done such and such,’ but say ‘Allah has decreed, and what He wills He does.’” Effort is seen and preserved (“and that his effort is going to be seen”), excellence is beloved to Allah, and “whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise.” And for what is hard: “O Allah, nothing is easy except what You make easy.”

now: Repeat: “O Allah, nothing is easy except what You make easy, and You make the difficult easy if You will”
Divide the material into small parts and start on the first part now
week: Make a realistic timetable with breaks and enough sleep
Keep your phone away while studying
Study with a serious classmate
long: If you fail: “Allah has decreed, and what He wills He does,” then analyse the causes and plan the next attempt
Make your intention to benefit people with your knowledge

questions: What is stopping me from focusing: fear? Distraction? Exhaustion?
If I fail, what is the backup plan?
avoid: Staying up all night before the exam

laziness.label: Procrastination and laziness
laziness.insight: “There are two blessings in which many people are deceived: health and free time,” and “take advantage of five before five.” The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge from “incapacity and laziness.” The Prophetic remedy for getting started: “The deeds most beloved to Allah are those done most consistently, even if few” — start small and keep going.

now: Choose one task and work on it for just 10 minutes, now
Pray: “O Allah, I seek refuge in You from incapacity and laziness”
week: Tie the task to a fixed time each day
Keep distractions (your phone) away during work time
long: Set a goal with a bigger meaning that moves you
Track your progress weekly

questions: Is the laziness from real exhaustion, or from fear of failure?

addiction.label: Addiction and bad habits
addiction.insight: Addiction is a kind of captivity, and Islam treats the one afflicted by it with realistic mercy: the door of repentance is open however often the sin is repeated (“the best of those who sin are those who repent”); change requires changing one's environment (the man who killed a hundred: “do not return to your land, for it is an evil land”); going astray comes in “steps”, so it is cut off at the first one; “whoever strives to be patient, Allah will make him patient”; and “you will never give up anything for the sake of Allah except that Allah will replace it with something better.” At the same time, physical addiction is a medical condition that needs specialised treatment.

now: Move away from the trigger now (close the device, leave the place)
Make wudu and pray two units of prayer
Talk to someone you trust
week: Identify your triggers: time, place, feelings (loneliness, boredom, pressure)
Put practical barriers in place (blocking software, changing your routine, getting rid of the substances)
Fill the gap with an alternative (exercise, company, learning)
long: If you relapse, do not despair; repent and start again immediately
Join a treatment programme or a support group
Look for righteous company to help you

questions: What feeling am I trying to escape through this habit?
What usually comes before a relapse?
Who could be my accountability partner?
avoid: Relying on willpower alone without changing the environment
Being ashamed to seek medical help
addiction.help: Addiction to drugs, alcohol and gambling are medical conditions with specialised treatment; seeking treatment is part of taking the means and does not contradict repentance.

desire.label: Desire and chastity
desire.insight: Desire is part of human nature, and the Sunnah's guidance for it is practical: marriage for those who are able, fasting for those who are not, lowering the gaze (“that is purer for them”), and “do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse” — that is, cut off the paths leading to it. The Prophet ﷺ reasoned mercifully with the young man who asked permission to commit zina: “Would you like it for your mother?” and prayed for him. And whoever resists temptation at its peak will have the shade of the Throne: “a man who is called by a woman of status and beauty and says: I fear Allah.”

now: Move away from the source of temptation immediately (a conversation, a place, an image)
Pray: “O Allah, purify my heart and guard my chastity”
week: Cut off unlawful channels of contact
Fast a day or two
Fill your time with exercise and good company
long: Work seriously towards marriage if you are able
Make lowering your gaze a daily habit

questions: What is the first step that usually leads me into the wrong?
If this happened with my sister or my daughter, how would I feel?
avoid: Giving in with the excuse that “it is natural”
Staying in situations of seclusion and temptation

death_fear.label: Fear of death and the Hereafter
death_fear.insight: Fear of death is natural, and the Prophetic way turns it into a motivation rather than a paralysis: “and let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow.” It balances fear and hope: “Inform My servants that it is I who am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that it is My punishment which is the painful punishment.” And “none of you should die except while thinking well of Allah.”

now: Think well of Allah, and read the verses about His mercy
week: Do a good deed you would love to meet Allah with
Return people's rights and write your will
long: Make the remembrance of death a motive for action, not a cause of anxiety

questions: What would I love to meet Allah upon?
